To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
breast cancer invasion is mediated in part by β-NAG, which is associated with dysregulation in secretory pathways of cancer cells.
cancer cell invasion is mediated by the action of β-NAG, and that this enzyme is dysregulated in the cancer cells and is secreted to act on extracellular matrix glycosidases.
the activity of β-NAG is increased in cancer cells and that this is associated with an increase in protease activity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the enzymes and the mechanism of action that are responsible for the invasion of breast cancer cells.
the role of the secretory pathway in cancer invasion, which is a poorly understood area.
the molecular mechanisms involved in the invasion process of cancer cells and how the extracellular matrix (ECM) is modified to facilitate this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cancer cells have altered their secretory pathways to allow for the production of glycosidases that can be secreted into the extracellular matrix to facilitate invasion of the tumor.
cancer cell invasion is mediated by the combined activities of β-NAG and proteases.
cancer cells are able to invade through the extracellular matrix by secreting β-NAG to expose the protein backbone and then the action by the proteases to create the space needed for cell movement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cancer cells secrete a variety of glycosidases and proteases to degrade the carbohydrate polymers that coat the protein backbone of the extracellular matrix.
cancer cells have an increased ability to secrete glycosylases that can cleave glycoconjugates in the extracellular matrix.

the cancer cell is a glycoprotein factory that produces glycoprotein enzymes that are secreted into the extracellular matrix to modify the glycoprotein content of the matrix and thereby promote cellular invasion.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the extracellular matrix (ECM) is not only a physical barrier for cancer cells to cross, but also an active barrier, as the carbohydrate polymers in the ECM are masked and the protein backbone is protected from proteolytic attack.
glycosidases play a role in cancer cell invasion.
cancer cells secrete glycosylases to modify their environment, and this is a critical step in the process of invasion and metastasis.
